drills.q: A teammate proposes a decaying epsilon schedule (eps_t=c/t) to fix epsilon-greedy's linear regret. Does this work, and what's the remaining downside?
drills.a: Yes, a properly decaying epsilon can achieve logarithmic regret matching UCB/Thompson asymptotically, but it reintroduces a hand-tuning problem (decay rate and schedule shape) that UCB/Thompson largely avoid -- too fast decays to a possibly-wrong arm prematurely, too slow keeps regret closer to the fixed-epsilon case for a long transient period.

drills.q: Why does UCB1's bonus term include ln(t) in the numerator rather than depending on n_i alone?
drills.a: The ln(t) term tightens the confidence bound as the total number of rounds grows, accounting for making more simultaneous confidence-interval claims across all arms over time -- without it, the exploration guarantee wouldn't hold uniformly as the horizon grows, a detail that matters for the formal regret proof even though n_i is the dominant term.

drills.q: A contextual bandit performs well on average but poorly for one specific, identifiable user segment. Diagnose.
drills.a: That segment's context region has likely been under-explored -- either the confidence bonus is poorly calibrated (lambda or alpha_bonus mistuned) or the segment is simply rare in traffic. Check per-segment cumulative regret specifically, not just aggregate regret, and consider a segment-specific or hierarchical prior for genuinely rare segments.

drills.q: Your bandit-driven pricing system occasionally serves a clearly bad price to a real customer. Is this a bug? What's the standard production fix?
drills.a: Not a bug -- it's inherent to any exploring bandit, which must occasionally choose a non-best-known option to gather information. Fix: an explicit safety floor (exclude options below an offline-vetted minimum quality/price threshold from the live exploration set) or a hard cap on the fraction of traffic exploration can consume.

drills.q: You're asked to add a contextual bandit to a currently-static recommendation ranker. What would you check before concluding this is the right addition?
drills.a: Confirm there's a genuine ongoing decision with real uncertainty (not a one-time variant choice better suited to a fixed A/B test); confirm sufficient informative context features exist to make LinUCB's added complexity worth it over plain UCB/Thompson; and confirm the org has operational maturity (safety floors, per-segment regret monitoring, off-policy eval) to safely run something that will occasionally serve suboptimal recommendations.

drills.q: LinUCB systematically underperforms in a setting with a strongly nonlinear context-reward relationship. How do you detect this, and is switching to a neural bandit the right fix?
drills.a: Detect by comparing, on logged data, how well a flexible nonlinear model (tree ensemble, neural net) predicts observed rewards versus the linear ridge model -- a large persistent gap that doesn't close with more data indicates the linear assumption (high bias) is the bottleneck. Before switching to a nonlinear bandit, check whether hand-engineered interaction/nonlinear features fed into the same LinUCB framework close most of the gap -- often sufficient and much simpler to maintain.

drills.q: What does inverse propensity scoring correct for in off-policy bandit evaluation, and what does it require to be valid?
drills.a: It reweights each logged reward by 1/P(old policy chose this action in this context), correcting for the old policy's own action-selection frequencies so the reweighted average unbiasedly estimates the new policy's expected reward. Requires knowing or reliably estimating the old policy's exact per-context action probabilities -- not always available for undocumented systems -- and the estimator's variance grows large when old and new policies disagree substantially.

drills.q: Is minimizing cumulative regret always the right objective for a production bandit?
drills.a: No -- if the actual business goal is 'identify the single best arm as fast as possible, accepting reward loss during a dedicated exploration phase' (the pure/best-arm-identification bandit variant), that's a different objective than cumulative regret minimization, and UCB/Thompson sampling (tuned for regret minimization while running) aren't the right algorithm family for it. Conflating the two objectives is a real, consequential mismatch.
